en: Paramārthasevā Sferra 2007b: Stanzas 1–4 actually appear on a single leaf (folio 1 verso), which is partially damaged at the bottom and contains approximately the first eight and a half stanzas (up to pāda c) of the work.

This folio was included among twenty other folios in a codex catalogued as MS 117 and microfilmed by the NGMPP on Reel C 13/5, which is labeled ‘Pañcarakṣā (Prakīrṇa)’ despite none of the folios appearing to contain the *Pañcarakṣā*. The folio containing the beginning of the *Paramārthasevā* consists of seven lines and is written in *gomola* script.

Stanzas 47–54 appear on folio 5 recto1 through 5 verso3. This constitutes part of a small group of four folios (folios 3 recto–6 verso) containing stanzas 21c–69c of the text. Specifically, folio 3r, which is partially broken, contains stanzas 21c–27c; folio 3 verso (partially broken) contains stanzas 27c–33c; folio 4r contains stanzas 33c–39d; folio 4v contains stanzas 39d–46b; and folio 5r contains stanzas [46c–54].

{46b–52c; fol. 5v, stanzas 52c–59a; fol. 6r, stanzas 59a–64d; fol. 6v, stanzas 64d–69c.} These leaves have been grouped with fifty-seven folios from a different manuscript (of the *Kriyāsaṅgrahapañjikā*), catalogued as MS 163 and microfilmed by the NGMPP on Reel C 17/7, which consists of sixty-one leaves, each containing five or six lines and measuring 31.5 × 9.5 cm.
It is written in the Gomola script and is labeled generically as "Bauddha Tantra.
Oṃ namo mañjunāthāya.
Having prostrated with my head to the glorious Śākyasiṃha, the sun of wisdom in the three realms,
and to the protector Maitreya and Mañjughoṣa;
Cintāmaṇi, Vajradhara, and Yaśas. || 1 ||

I shall describe that service to the Supreme Reality, which is inaccessible to men of dull intellect through the various doctrines of the six philosophical systems or by means of logic and other such methods.
Having briefly destroyed the worldly views. || 2 ||

The attainment of desired success follows from the mouth of the teacher in the entirety of the Vajrayāna sung by the Omniscient One; therefore, the teacher should be regarded as gold by his beloved disciples.
When examined, not even a trace of sin exists. || 3 ||
Having abandoned that Vajrasattva, the father, in whom there existed Hari, Brahmā, Rudra, the moon, the sun, Rāhu, the planets, the stars, and so forth;
Fools follow the path of the dull-witted world. || 4 ||
...devoid of valid means of knowledge.
(Sferra 2007a:
Indeed, worldly discourse consists of various kinds of distinctions in views and doctrines.

The Veda is beyond reasoning and the Smṛtis are divided; what, then, should a virtuous person in this world accept? (5) 5a Tib.: "In this world, the certainty of words is deficient in logic... 5d gṛhṇātu conjecture.
May they accept [it], O N. However, it is worth noting that *sādhujanaḥ* is translated into Tibetan as a plural:
*mkhas pa rnams*.
For those who proclaim the meaning of the words sung by the Omniscient One will speak one thing, while others will speak another due to their many diverse opinions.
The teachers established in the six philosophical systems are well known; they are awakened by the elements (*dhātu*) and asleep in the equilibrium of the elements.
(6) Having heard the tantra, yet being devoid of the teacher’s oral instruction, one is uninitiated and lost on the path of the syllables (*akṣara*).
What consideration can there be for that fool who assumes the office of a great teacher?

(7) Greedy for wealth and desire, he bestows initiation; he draws his own maṇḍala with colored powders; he worships a stone image as his chosen *liṅga*; and he offers clarified butter and other substances into the fire of a sacrificial pit. (8)
"Oṃkāra-hūṃkāra"—thus [it is said]; this is stated as the desired mantra, whereas that other [mantra] is merely common (*prākṛta*).
One whose intellect is ruined does not know it thus: for that which is merely sound is indeed the mantra. (9)
9a. *ohūṃkāram* N; *ohūṃkāram* G. *itīo* N; *itāo* G. 9d. *mantram* N, Tib.; *mātram* G.
A rogue heron, having entered a lake where there were no royal swans, attained a semblance of beauty amidst the cluster of lotuses.
A wicked teacher among people is like a hidden death within his own family, just as [death is] among fish.
(10) 10a *praviṣṭaḥ* em.; *praviṣṭa* G; *praviṣṭe* N. 10b *obhāṃ gato* (or *obhāṅ gato*) *dhūrtavako* N; [text] broken in G. 10c *jhaṣāo* N (*jhasāo*); *<jha>sāo* G. 10d *ogurur* N; *oguru<r>* G.
Constricting his throat while perched upon lotus petals with one foot, this rogue creates the illusion that these are fish; he is like a wicked teacher who deludes the people.
Seated upon a single lotus petal,
like an actor who, for the sake of the dramatic sentiment (*bhāva*) in a play, assumes the form of the Lord of the Gods (*surendra*) for his role.
Likewise, one who is greedy for wealth and desire, being on a wrong path, performs an initiation that involves binding the crown of the head with a Jina.
(12) Just as an actor... (12ab) ...for this reason he acts... (12c) ...the binding... (12d) ...one who is on a wrong path, greedy for wealth and desire.
Afflicted by desire, intoxicated by liquor, heedless, with a mind full of anger,
greedy for great wealth, a speaker of untruth, and seeking to deceive his disciples— that teacher who causes suffering is no wonder at all. (13)
13c. *sūtao* em. *sūtao* N; *śrutao* G. 13d. *ogurur* N] *oguru<r>* G. *citram* N] *cittram* G.

Seized by the Teacher—who stands upon the Great Path—for the sake of destroying the torment of one scorched by the fire of the suffering of *saṃsāra* and blinded by darkness, [the Teacher was grasped] like a sleeping snake [mistaken for something else] through delusion regarding poison. (14)

14ab: [The text] is heated by the Guru; [the word] *timira* is found in G (*timiraio* in N). 14c: *ostho* in G (conjectured by KIELHORN as *osthe*); *ostho* in N. 14d: *osarpaḥ* in N; *osayyaḥ* in G.ac.
By many foolish people, whose minds are greedy for the bliss of Nirvāṇa, [it is explained] through various other doctrines.
For what purpose is a wicked teacher propitiated, when, upon being examined, he is one who bestows hell and other such realms?
(15) 15a *dharmāntarair* [G, Tib. : *karmāturaiḥ* [N] 15bc *ottaiḥ* | *ārādhito* [N] : [fragmented in G] *oguruḥ* [N] : *guruḥ* [G] 15d *parīkṣyaḥ* [em. : *parīkṣyaḥ* [GN].
Having transcended the states of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, established in wisdom, and inseparable from compassion and the other [perfections],
he is without sense faculties, eternal, inconceivable, without lineage, all-pervading, and utterly peaceful. (16)
He is the venerable Vajrasattva, he is the Ādibuddha, and he is the venerable Mañjughoṣa, the Lord of the World; he is inconceivable and beyond logic.
He is the illustrious Vajraḍāka, the Mind-Vajra, the imperishable one, to be realized through the yoga of the partless. (17) *Note:

Between verses 17 and 18, the manuscript N contains the following two pādas, which are not present in G or the Tibetan translation:* He is the supreme lord of all mantras, the great mantra-knowledge-holder, the sovereign of all mantras, and the master of all mantras.
He is the source of all, the vajra that is the cause of existence; he is Ādinātha, the Sugata, the Lord of Jinas.
He is Īśvara, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha; he is the destroyer of Māra, the Sugata, the Lord of Jinas.
He is the glorious Śākyasiṃha and the sage Yaśas; he is the glorious Kālacakra and the omniscient Buddha.
(18) He is the Lord, the beloved of Viṣṇu, and the Great Grandfather (*pitāmaha*).
That venerable Guru is indeed manifested as peaceful, a hidden Buddha, a bestower of happiness upon the earth;
he alone is the enemy of Māra, the sole kinsman of the world, and a wish-fulfilling gem for those who serve the true Guru. (19)
19a. *oguru* N; *oguru<r>* G. 19b. *pracchannabuddhaḥ suo* N; [broken] in G. *dharaṇyām* G; *dharaṇyā* N. 19c. *obandhuś* N; *ovandhu* G. 19d. *sadguruo* N; *saṃsutao* G. *osevao* N; [broken] in G.
A meditator, liberated from attachment through meditation, yet possessing desire with a mind bound by great longing;
one who observes the great vow, whose passion remains undestroyed even in the union with a mudrā for the sake of the bliss of the two organs.
(20) 20 This stanza is quoted in the GBh, p. 87. 20a *ovimukta*o NGBh ] *ovinaṣṭa*o G. 20b.
okāmao GN; okākamao N; onibaddhao NGBh; ovivuddhao G. 2 20c mahāvratī dvīndriopc ac N; broken in G.
Having lost his yoga on the path of the moon and sun, he has entered the fire of wisdom through the power of yoga.
He alone is the venerable Guru, the Holder of the Vajra, the destroyer of evil, who is the very sprinkling of the nectar of infinite bliss. (21)
Greedy for a single [act of] giving, he does not beg; having avoided a virtuous son, he is not a renouncer of wealth that has come easily.
He does not seek the accumulation of the riches he has obtained, but rather makes use of the wealth once it is acquired. (22)
22a *satsutao* em. *satsu tao* G; *satsuo* N (contra metrum); *vivarjya* N] *vivarkku* (?
G 22b This pāda is quoted in the KS, fol. 2v2; *dānasya* N] *dāna* (! G (contra metrum) 22d *oni vittāny* N] *nimittāny* G; *upao* N] *uya* (!)o G.
The teacher of the unsurpassed songs of Tantra, the remover of cyclic existence for his virtuous sons,
who displays [the realms] up to the world of Brahmā within his own body— he is the glorious Guru, the glorious Guru alone, and none other. (23)
He is perfectly revealed by infinite Buddhas and is constantly honored and saluted by the Bodhisattvas dwelling in all directions.
He has been praised by the Siddhas with many vajra-songs as the one who reveals the goal of liberation; be [like him], O Inconceivable One, from falling [into the cycle of existence].
(24) 24d Tib.: [He is] the guide on the path for those fallen into the wilderness of existence. % PDSZ: *mokṣārtha* refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Kaiser.

The venerable Guru is not one who falls into the void of existence; the venerable Guru is not one who gazes upon the path to liberation [out of worldly motives]; the venerable Guru is not one who craves vulgar desires; the venerable Guru is not one greedy for wealth that comes easily; the venerable Guru is not one who slanders virtuous people; the venerable Guru is not one devoid of compassion for sentient beings. (25)

The true Guru is not one who bestows wealth from the property of the Saṅgha; the true Guru is not one who abandons a disciple who is destitute; the true Guru is not one who assigns tasks according to his own whims; the true Guru is not one who enforces silence upon a virtuous son. (26)
The Śrī Guru is not one who conceals the reality of his virtuous sons;
the Śrī Guru is not one who seeks to deceive his virtuous sons. The Saṅgha... [text fragment]. The Śrī Guru is not one who deceives his virtuous sons.
The glorious guru does not obstruct the long-term welfare of his virtuous sons; the glorious guru does not seek the abandonment of his virtuous sons.
(27) The glorious guru is not arrogant due to the power of his knowledge; the glorious guru is not delighted by the power of material wealth.
The venerable Guru does not seek the aims of petty households; the venerable Guru has not entered into the pleasures of sovereignty. || 28 ||
28c *kṣudragṛhāśramārthī* (conj. based on Tib. *khyim du bsti bdod 'dod*) ] *kṣudragṛhāśra(—)nvī* N;
*kṣudragṛhāśrayārthī* Kaiser. 471.
The venerable Guru is not one who wears a sacred thread around his own neck; the venerable Guru is indeed not one who carries a Vaiṣṇava staff;
the venerable Guru is not one whose limbs are smeared with ashes; the venerable Guru is not one with long matted hair, nor does he wear a girdle of muñja grass.
(29) 29c em. *ogātro* ] *ogātra* N.
The venerable guru does not wear a shaven head and a skull-bowl; the venerable guru is not naked with shorn hair;
the venerable guru does not have his body covered by a red robe; the venerable guru is not bound by a yogic cloth.
(30) Between pādas b and c, the Tibetan version contains the following pāda: "By virtue of solitude..."
The verse *dga' dpal ldan bla ma min* (2.30c) is quoted in the *Kālacakra-sādhana* (KS), fol. 3r7, which continues as follows:
*na śrīgurū śikhākirīṭapātradhārihastaḥ* (sic; cf. st. 33b). Together with pādas 34a and 33d (see below):
*yogapaṭaprabaddhaḥ* (em.; *yogapaṭāprabaddhaḥ* N). The Tibetan translation reads as follows:
The Śrī Guru is not one who is tightly bound by the embrace of pus; the Śrī Guru is not intoxicated by the power of liquor;
the Śrī Guru does not have a mind corrupted by [the desire for] living beings; the Śrī Guru is not one exulting under the sway of sensual pleasure. (31)

Between verses 31 and 32, there is the following pāda in the Tibetan: "One who is attached to the pleasure of transformation is not the glorious guru" (verse 31d). Oruḥ saukhyavaśāt prahṛṣṭaḥ is partially broken in N.
%PDSZ: gurur madyavaśāt is broken off.
The noble Guru does not despond under the power of suffering; the noble Guru is not negligent on the path to liberation.
The noble Guru’s mind is not lost to the path; the noble Guru is not destroyed by any affliction.
The glorious guru is not one who causes suffering to his own senses; the glorious guru is not one who carries a skull-bowl.

The glorious guru is not one who dwells in the open air, nor is the glorious guru one who dwells at the foot of a tree. (33) 33b This pāda is quoted in the *Kāyasthiti-sādhana* (cf. Moriguchi 1998: 76). 33d This pāda is quoted in the *Kāyasthiti-sādhana*, fol. 3r7. *pādapao* KS; *pāpadapao* N (contrary to the meter).

[With] his own senses... [broken off]; holding a bowl in his hand; Kaiser; fol. 4r: open space; Kaiser: dwelling at the feet [of the master]; The venerable Guru does not wear a miserable rag-robe, nor does the venerable Guru eat as a mendicant at fixed times; the venerable Guru does not dwell in desolate, inaccessible places, nor does the venerable Guru enter mountain caves. ||O|| (34)

He who has abandoned the faults of existence is the glorious guru; he is not the glorious guru who eats at the proper time [but lacks virtue]. (34ab) This *pāda* is quoted in the *Kālachakra-sādhana* (KS), fol. 3r7. The Tibetan translation for 34b is: "A monk who eats at the proper time is not the glorious guru. Sanskrit: *sa śrīgurur yo bhavadoṣanaṣṭaḥ* | (He is the glorious guru who has abandoned the faults of existence.)
He is the venerable guru who speaks pleasant words; he is the venerable guru who points out the auspicious path.
(35ab) He whose [defilements] have been destroyed by the incense of virtues—[he is the one].
(35d) *oḥ śubhamārgadeśī* is reconstructed based on the Tibetan *lam bzaṅ*.
He who removes the fire of hell is the glorious Guru; he who leads one across the ocean of existence is the glorious Guru;
he who is the sole kinsman of the world is the glorious Guru; he who is the sole eye of the world is the glorious Guru. (36)
That glorious Guru,
who is the sole mother of the world; that glorious Guru, who is the sole lord of the world.
He is the venerable Guru who is the unique moon of the world; he is the venerable Guru who is the unique sun of the world.
(37) 37a This pāda is not translated into Tibetan. ^472
He is the glorious guru who knows the meaning of the Sugata; he is the glorious guru who destroys the inexhaustible Māra;
he is the glorious guru who bestows the inexhaustible path; he is the glorious guru who subdues the inexhaustible Māra.
He is the venerable Guru who wears the sacred thread upon his neck; he is the venerable Guru who holds the staff of the Imperishable;
he is the venerable Guru whose limbs are covered with the dust of virtues; he is the venerable Guru who has bound the crown of the Jina upon his head.
(39) He is the venerable Guru who bears a shaven body; he is the venerable Guru whose hair has been shorn by the enemy.
He is the venerable guru who is immersed in the suffering of existence; he is the venerable guru whose body is veiled by the foremost cloth.
(40) He is the venerable guru who longs for the vessel of nectar; he is the venerable guru who has entered the observance (*samaya*).
He is the venerable guru who seeks to protect the body; he is the venerable guru who possesses the breath and the sacrificial thread. (41)

He is a venerable guru who dwells at the foot of the Jina-tree; he is a venerable guru whose hand holds the vessel of vows. He is a venerable guru who sleeps on a bed of grass; he is a venerable guru who eats at the fixed time. He is a venerable guru who has entered the forest-dwelling; he is a venerable guru who resides in a mountain cave.
He is the venerable guru who possesses a mind of equanimity toward all beings; he is the venerable guru who, through the triple purity, bestows fearlessness.
(43) Is that venerable guru not indeed to be served? Is that venerable guru not indeed to be gratified? (43d) *abhayadaḥ* em.; *abhayadāḥ* N.
Is that glorious guru not indeed worthy of worship? Is that glorious guru not indeed worthy of salutation?

(44) He is the bestower of happiness through beds, seats, vehicles, slaves, and servants; through celestial women of exquisite beauty; with kinsmen, beloved wives, and sons; and even with his own head. (45)
With beautiful women,
with rice cooked in milk, meat, and ghee, with fragrant foods and drinks, many and delightful,
and with betel, camphor, and excellent mouth-perfumes— [N7 missing].
[The one] with many Māras as enemies [is protected] by musk and other [substances].
(46) 46d Tib.: by means of musk and so forth, [it is for] the many Māras, the enemies.
Adorned with long pendants,
jeweled earrings, girdles, anklets, and bracelets;
Wearing armlets, bracelets, and necklaces, and clad in variegated garments, he is the remover of the suffering of existence.
With ointments such as saffron and sandalwood, with incenses such as black aloe-wood and *śihlaka*,
with fragrant flowers such as the excellent *campaka*, and with jewel-lamps, his path remains unobstructed.
Due to the influence of the Kali age, a teacher may be a mixture of virtues and faults; indeed, he should never be considered entirely free from sin.
However, one who possesses superior qualities and has been thoroughly examined should be the one to be honored by your sons. (49)
A Buddha made of stone or even wood does not grant liberation for hundreds of thousands of lifetimes;
however, a Guru, through his devotion, bestows eternal bliss even in this very life. (50)

There is no mother or father equal to the Guru; nor is there a brother or a wife who is as true a friend and protector as he. He, the Holder of the Vajra, bestows excellent fortune that destroys suffering even in this very life. (51)
He should be propitiated with a perfectly pure intellect, so that he does not become a source of suffering even with the passage of time;
for those of impure mind, [his] propitiation results in suffering, like the drinking of clarified butter when a fever has intensified. 52.
It is better not to have made a guru at all for the sake of pleasure by those of ruined minds, for he brings much suffering;
rather, the renunciation of a desired fruit beforehand is better than the pain of falling far from the foot of a tree.
Better is the face of Yama when greatly enraged, or even that of a venomous serpent, or of a five-faced great elephant, than that of a teacher due to the lack of discipline in a wicked disciple. 54.
The face of the glorious guru, when propitiated, is desired; when provoked, it is undesirable for hundreds of lifetimes.
Therefore, having reflected well with one’s own intelligence, he should be propitiated and never provoked. (55)
Those who are greedy for this world and the next worship images made of stone or wood;
yet they revile that Great Guru, who is sentient and the abode of all virtues.
(56) 56d *odūṣayanti* em. ] *odūṣayantī* N.

They are constantly seized by obstacles and Vināyakas, and by many Māras who are guardians of the fires of hell—those who, having abandoned their own mind which is the manifest Lord of Jinas, worship that which is insentient. (57) 57d *paripūjayanti* is conjectured based on the Tibetan (*mchod byed*). *ye* is emended; *jeye* appears in N (though it violates the meter).

They fulfill [the qualities], O Mañjuśrī; for the primordial Tathāgatas perform worship of another Teacher. What is the reason? It is for the sake of training sentient beings, and not because they are desirous of attaining liberation for themselves. (58)
58c. *kiṃo* em. ] *kaṃo* N; *ovineyao* em. ] *ovinayao* N (contrary to the meter); 58d. *mokṣaṃ* N ] *nirvāṇamokṣaṃ* N.ac.
In this way, the Guru installs the desired *liṅga* for the sake of merit for the ignorant world;
he performs worship and many salutations, yet not out of greed for the state of *nirvāṇa*. (59)
This body, wife, children, and the multitude of many kinsmen are indeed impermanent;
so too are grain, wealth, sovereignty, and even the state of being free from enemies, as well as the states of being a perfected one (*siddha*), a Buddha, or a sage (*ṛṣi*).
(60) 60d The word *buddha* is translated into Tibetan as *dbaṅ po*.
If you perceive any imperishable thing here among these— the cause of intense delusion and passion—
whether stationary or moving within the three realms, such that no form of entity shall ever go to destruction;
Take heed, for this body of yours must be watched over until death awakens it;
once it has awakened, it delivers its body to birds, jackals, and elephants. (62)
In this way, wife, son, kinsman, friend, protector, and one who has come for refuge—
even when given by Time to the flames and other such things— Indra and the other gods are not capable of protecting them. (63)

Because they were given by Time, even the perfected sages and the lords of the gods, numbering as many as the infinite, have been brought to destruction. Who is capable of warding off one's own karma, as long as the fire of knowledge remains unseen? (64)
All this is indeed impermanent and undesirable; the nectar of knowledge from the mouth of the venerable Guru is desirable.
Since both of these are the source of suffering and pleasure, why do you not accept [the latter] after due reflection?
(65) While you perform worship of your own body, which by its very nature causes wandering through the miserable wilderness of saṃsāra.

Why indeed do you not offer that very [woman] to the Guru, who bestows the entirety of the bliss of nirvāṇa? (66) Having given away wealth acquired by yourself, why do you take for yourself a woman who delivers one to the fires of hell?
Why do you not give that auspicious woman to the Guru, she who grants the embrace of a Buddha’s consort? (67)
By the power of merit, celestial maidens come to be, as well as delightful wealth and grain; yet by the influence of evil, even those things long accumulated and well-guarded go to ruin. (68)
Therefore, one should give gifts that are distinguished and pleasing to the mind at the feet of the Guru;
for those [gifts] which have been bestowed will surely grant happiness even in many future births. (69)
The gifts that have been given bear fruit, just as seeds do in very pure soil; those not given do not bear fruit at all, like seeds in barren ground. (70)
Just as a fool undergoes extreme hardship for the sake of crops in fields that lack seeds,
so too one who desires to seize the wealth not given by his teacher wanders upon the earth. (71)
474 71b *otyanta* karoti [sic metri causa for *otyantaṃ karoti*] 2 71c *tathā* conj. based on the context and Tib. (*de bźin du*) ] *yathā* N.
Greedy for wealth and desire, he performs service, engages in agriculture, and acquires knowledge;
yet poverty remains for a long time with that evildoer, swiftly returning again and again.
(72) 72a *kṛṣiṃ* N Tib. (field); should one read *kṛśām*?

For one who performs great merit, crops, gold, and wives appear even without effort; inconceivable attainments—such as the state of a Siddha, Indra, or a Rishi, and the supreme sovereignty of a foeless king that bestows happiness upon the earth—all whatever is auspicious within the three realms, comes entirely through the power of pleasing the Guru. (73)
Poverty, disease, and the intense suffering of the fires of hell arise from dissatisfaction with that [teacher].
Thus, in the *Uttaratantra* sung by the Tathāgatas, it is said that through the grace of the Guru, the desired accomplishment is attained;
yet in another tantra, this statement stands: "Due to dissatisfaction with him, one enters hell. (74–75)

Having recognized the Guru as one whose mind is filled with excellent qualities, those who abandon him even for the sake of cyclic existence— *Uttaratantra*, N; *uttaratantre*, N*; *ogītā*, em.; *ogītaṃ*, N. *etad*, conj. (cf. Tib. *’di ñid ni*); *etta*, N. *narake*, N; *narakā*, N*.pc ac. *jñātvā guruṃ sadguṇapūrṇacittaṃ saṃsārahetor api ye tyajanti* |
For infinite eons, deprived of happiness, they are cooked in the hell of the blazing vajra-fire. (76) 76d. In the hell (narake), [they] fall (patanti).

It is not only the disciples there who are cooked—those who have acquired evil and deceived the true Guru—but the Guru as well, ruined by the power of greed, has entered the blazing fire of passion and the like. This suffering is common to both when the Guru and the disciple are ruined. (77)
Therefore, a teacher who has here become lost to his disciple must be avoided from afar by means of his own discernment. (78)
It is better to seize a furious serpent, a lion with diamond-like claws in a state of intoxication,
a fierce-faced eight-legged beast with sharp fangs, than a teacher and disciple who have lost their way. (79) [Is it "with his disciples"?]
The disciple does not fall from the downfall of the guru, nor is the guru lost through the downfall of the disciple.
For one who has climbed a tree with long branches, if a fall occurs, he goes to his death. (80) The fourteen downfalls from the *Anuttaratantra-gītā* destroy accomplishment along with their roots.
For infinite eons, they have been deprived of happiness!
[81] [81c] *osaukhyāḥ*: the final syllable is not clearly legible. [81d] Tibetan: "He spoke to the disciples who were empowered and abiding in evil karma."
For a disciple who has been initiated but follows a wrong path, there is a single downfall resulting from distressing the mind of the guru. (81d)
The second [is incurred] due to the abandonment of commands;
the third, due to speaking out of anger toward one's brother; and the fourth, due to the abandonment of friendliness. 82bis.

The sixth [downfall] is called "arrow" for abandoning the glorious bodhicitta; the seventh is called "tree" for grasping at faults in the established tenets; and [the eighth] is called "mountain" for conversing with one who is not a mantra-practitioner.
